1 big thing: Gaming biz could get a GTA bump
 
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios

Millions of gamers will likely spend some time this holiday weekend with Grand Theft Auto VI — a blockbuster hit that could reinvigorate an industry desperate for growth, Axios' Sara Fischer and Kerry Flynn write.

  • Rockstar Games' hotly anticipated game generated an estimated $3.79 billion in sales on its first day alone.

🖼️ The big picture: Gaming hardware sales have slowed dramatically in recent years amid a maturing console generation and price hikes driven in part by chip shortages.

  • Global Xbox hardware sales fell nearly 65% between 2023 and 2025, while PlayStation sales fell almost 20%, per VGChartz.

🕹️ GTA VI is available on Sony's PlayStation 5 and Microsoft's Xbox Series X and S consoles, giving consumers a reason to buy new hardware or upgrade their setup.

  • Bart Spiegel, PwC's global entertainment and media leader, tells Axios: "A release of this magnitude can motivate people to invest in their entertainment setups and deepen their engagement with gaming, creating spending habits that extend well beyond the initial launch."
Data: VGChartz. Chart: Axios Visuals

💸 Between the lines: Axios alumnus Stephen Totilo, owner, editor and writer of Game File, says that game developers are grappling with ballooning production budgets, making it more difficult to recoup their investments and contributing to widespread layoffs.

  • GTA VI took more than eight years to develop and reportedly cost more than $1 billion, per Bloomberg.

But PwC's Spiegel says the game's runaway success could renew investor interest across the gaming world.

  • He tells Axios: "Ultimately, GTA VI's greatest economic contribution may be its ability to strengthen the gaming market as a whole, rather than simply drive sales for a single franchise."

2. 🚦 Smarter traffic lights
 
Nashville has 200+ lidar sensors monitoring traffic, without the privacy concerns of license plate-reading cameras. Image: Ouster

Laser-sensing technology is being paired with AI to make traffic lights smarter, Axios' Joann Muller reports.

  • Smart traffic lights can give slower pedestrians more time to cross, or keep cars moving when nobody's waiting.

🚙 Driving the news: Nashville is expanding its deployment of lidar-based traffic technology from Ouster, adding 100 intersections to an existing network.

  • Ouster's BlueCity system uses lidar sensors to create detailed 3D images of traffic movements, which AI software analyzes in real time.

📷 The system can detect movement up to 500 feet away and capture color information, letting it distinguish between traffic signal colors.

3. 💡 Last-minute advice
 
Illustration: Andrea Chronopoulos for The New York Times

The lead story of today's New York Times business section is time-capsule-ready: "How to Talk With Your Family About A.I. Doom at Thanksgiving." San Francisco-based tech reporter Emmy Martin talked to AI researchers about what they'll bring up and how they'll parry questions.

  • Daniel Kokotajlo — a former OpenAI governance researcher who leads the AI Futures Project, known for the widely read "AI 2027" — feels obligated to say something at dinner with his wife's family in Boston.

"It feels like maybe I'm doing something wrong if I let the social awkwardness prevent me from bringing it up," said Kokotajlo, 34.

  • Around 2020, he gave the family a presentation on how quickly AI was improving. Now he thinks next year's holiday season will be "one with lots of AI-powered euphoria and whole new gadgets." (Don't ask about later years.)

🎙️ Another piece in today's Times rounds up thoughts from the paper's journalists about how they navigate polarizing topics at holiday gatherings.

  • Michael Barbaro, host of "The Daily," said: "I've definitely become my family's receptacle for anger at The Times."
  • White House correspondent Erica L. Green offered an all-purpose riposte: "Who wants another drink?!"

4. 📸 Pic to go: Shuttle stands
 
Photo: David Swanson/AFP via Getty Images

L.A.'s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center recently began welcoming visitors to one of the world's most impressive displays of science history: NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavour, vertically stacked as if taking off.

  • Former astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com of the nearly 200-foot-tall display: "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time."

🚀 Endeavour was built to replace Challenger. It last flew in 2011.

  • It's now one of four orbiters and test shuttles on display nationwide.

See the exhibit.
